content.comment_body: Hello, As you know, the [product_name] ([article_no]) features 4 high-speed inputs capable of 5kHz operation. I believe the typical cycle time for [product_name] is approximately 25 Hz. My question is: how does [product_name] detect digital signals on these high-speed inputs? I've used the attached file to test the system cycle time in simulation mode.

The [article_no] offers 4 high-speed counter (HSC) inputs. The assignment for which inputs support this function is fixed; it is I3, I4, I5, and I6. No software configuration is needed—these inputs always operate in fast mode, whether used for HSC or standard digital input. Internally, the inputs likely trigger a hardware interrupt to the processor, making their operation independent of the user program cycle time. Otherwise, during regular processing, [product_name] would be able to finish a cycle in less than 200 microseconds (1 / 5000).

Thank you [user_name]. So this means: 1. High-speed inputs work independently of the cycle time. 2. If I connect input I3, for example, to a counter, the counter operates correctly? Could you share a simple example program? Thanks in advance for the support.

Adding to the previous points: To count high-frequency pulses, you should connect one of the four high-speed inputs (I3-I6) directly to an up/down counter or a threshold trigger function block. This can be set up straightforwardly. From my experience, only when the inputs are directly connected to either of these two function blocks does [product_name] reliably register all pulses (as also mentioned in the manual). If you include additional function blocks (such as AND, OR, etc.) between the input and the counter/threshold trigger, the maximum count frequency will drop—likely to below 1kHz, slower than the 5kHz capability. For pulse counting and simply showing speed or distance in a message, it works (e.g., with ultrasonic sensors). However, for applications needing precise encoder measurements or regulation, [product_name] might be too slow.
